<div class = "blue">

### Learning Objectives

* Describe the purpose of the **`dplyr`** and **`tidyr`** packages.
* Select certain columns in a data frame with the **`dplyr`** function `select`.
* Select certain rows in a data frame according to filtering conditions with the **`dplyr`** function `filter`.
* Link the output of one **`dplyr`** function to the input of another function with the 'pipe' operator `%>%`.
* Add new columns to a data frame that are functions of existing columns with `mutate`.
* Use the split-apply-combine concept for data analysis.
* Use `summarize`, `group_by`, and `count` to split a data frame into groups of observations, apply a summary statistics for each group, and then combine the results.

</div>

## Data Manipulation using **`dplyr`** and **`tidyr`**

Bracket subsetting is handy, but it can be cumbersome and difficult to read,
especially for complicated operations. Enter **`dplyr`**. **`dplyr`** is a package for
making tabular data manipulation easier. It pairs nicely with **`tidyr`** which enables you to swiftly convert between different data formats for plotting and analysis.

Packages in R are basically sets of additional functions that let you do more
stuff. The functions we've been using so far, like `str()` or `data.frame()`,
come built into R; packages give you access to more of them. Before you use a
package for the first time you need to install it on your machine, and then you
should import it in every subsequent R session when you need it. You should
already have installed the **`tidyverse`** package. This is an
"umbrella-package" that installs several packages useful for data analysis which
work together well such as **`tidyr`**, **`dplyr`**, **`ggplot2`**, **`tibble`**, etc.

The **`tidyverse`** package tries to address 3 major problems with some of base R functions:

1. The results from a base R function sometimes depend on the type of data.
2. Using R expressions in a non standard way, which can be confusing for new learners.
3. Hidden arguments, having default operations that new learners are not aware of.

To load the package type:


```{r, message = FALSE, purl = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library("tidyverse")    ## load the tidyverse packages, incl. dplyr
```

### What are **`dplyr`** and **`tidyr`**?

The package **`dplyr`** provides easy tools for the most common data manipulation
tasks. It is built to work directly with data frames, with many common tasks
optimized by being written in a compiled language (C++). An additional feature is the
ability to work directly with data stored in an external database. The benefits of
doing this are that the data can be managed natively in a relational database,
queries can be conducted on that database, and only the results of the query are
returned.

This addresses a common problem with R in that all operations are conducted
in-memory and thus the amount of data you can work with is limited by available
memory. The database connections essentially remove that limitation in that you
can connect to a database of many hundreds of GB, conduct queries on it directly, and pull
back into R only what you need for analysis.

The package **`tidyr`** addresses the common problem of wanting to reshape your data for plotting and use by different R functions. Sometimes we want data sets where we have one row per measurement. Sometimes we want a data frame where each measurement type has its own column, and rows are instead more aggregated groups - like countries or decades. Moving back and forth between these formats is nontrivial, and **`tidyr`** gives you tools for this and more sophisticated  data manipulation.

To learn more about **`dplyr`** and **`tidyr`** after the workshop, you may want to check out this
[handy data transformation with **`dplyr`** cheatsheet](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/data-transformation.pdf) and this [one about **`tidyr`**](https://github.com/rstudio/cheatsheets/blob/main/tidyr.pdf).

## Our data: international environmental agreements

For the next two weeks we'll work with a new dataset: the [International Environmental Agreements (IEA) Database](https://www.iea.ulaval.ca), which tracks every treaty, protocol, and amendment that countries have signed to manage the environment, from 19th-century agreements about fishing on border rivers to the Montreal Protocol and the UN climate convention. The database was built by political scientist Ronald Mitchell at the University of Oregon and is now hosted by Université Laval. We'll use a simplified subset of it, frozen as of October 2026 and trimmed to a handful of columns for teaching. It comes as three linked tables:

* `iea_agreements.csv`: one row per agreement (this week)
* `iea_memberships.csv`: one row per country per agreement it has signed or joined (next week)
* `iea_countries.csv`: one row per country (next week)

The [codebook](https://ucd-rdavis.github.io/R-DAVIS/data/iea_codebook.md) describes every column. Missing values (`NA`) are left in on purpose: real data have gaps, and part of the job is figuring out where they are.

We'll read in our data using the `read_csv()` function, from the tidyverse package **`readr`**, instead of `read.csv()`, the base function for reading in data. We'll read it straight from the course website, but you can also download it into the `data` folder of your R_DAVIS_2026 project.

```{r,results = 'hide', purl = FALSE}
agreements <- read_csv("https://ucd-rdavis.github.io/R-DAVIS/data/iea_agreements.csv")

## inspect the data
str(agreements)
```

Notice that the class of the data is now `tbl_df`
This is referred to as a "tibble".
Tibbles are almost identical to R's standard data frames, but they tweak some of the old behaviors of data frames. For our purposes the only differences between data frames
and tibbles are that:

1. When you print a tibble, R displays the data type of each column under its name; it prints only the first few rows of data and only as many columns as fit
on one screen.
2. Columns of class `character` are never automatically converted into factors.

Each of the 5,016 rows is one agreement. A few columns we'll lean on:

* `scope`: `Bilateral` (between two countries), `Multilateral` (three or more), or `Other`
* `subject`: the issue area, like `Fish and fisheries` or `Pollution`
* `year_signed` and `year_in_force`: when the agreement was signed, and when it took effect (enough countries had ratified it)
* `n_members`: the number of countries the agreement has entered into force for

## Selecting columns and filtering rows

We're going to learn some of the most common **`dplyr`** functions: `select()`,
`filter()`, `mutate()`, `group_by()`, and `summarize()`. To select columns of a
data frame, use `select()`. The first argument to this function is the data
frame (`agreements`), and the subsequent arguments are the **columns** to keep.

```{r, results = 'hide', purl = FALSE}
select(agreements, agreement_name, year_signed, n_members)
```

To choose **rows** based on a specific criteria, use `filter()`. Here are all the agreements signed in 1992, the year of the Rio Earth Summit:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
filter(agreements, year_signed == 1992)
```

`filter` is used for **rows** and `select` is used for **columns**.

## Pipes

What if you want to select and filter at the same time? There are three
ways to do this: use intermediate steps, nested functions, or pipes.

With intermediate steps, you create a temporary data frame and use
that as input to the next function, like this:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements2 <- filter(agreements, n_members > 150)
agreements_big <- select(agreements2, agreement_name, year_signed, n_members)
```

This is readable, but can clutter up your workspace with lots of objects that you have to name individually. With multiple steps, that can be hard to keep track of.

You can also nest functions (i.e. one function inside of another), like this:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements_big <- select(filter(agreements, n_members > 150), agreement_name, year_signed, n_members)
```

This is handy, but can be difficult to read if too many functions are nested, as
R evaluates the expression from the inside out (in this case, filtering, then selecting).

The last option is **`pipes`**. Pipes let you take
the output of one function and send it directly to the next, which is useful
when you need to do many things to the same dataset.  Pipes in R look like
`%>%` and are made available via the **`magrittr`** package, installed automatically
with **`dplyr`**. If you use RStudio, you can type the pipe with <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>
+ <kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd> if you have a PC or <kbd>Cmd</kbd> +
<kbd>Shift</kbd> + <kbd>M</kbd> if you have a Mac.

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  filter(n_members > 150) %>%
  select(agreement_name, year_signed, n_members)
```

In the above code, we use the pipe to send the `agreements` dataset first through
`filter()` to keep rows where `n_members` is greater than 150, then through `select()`
to keep only the `agreement_name`, `year_signed`, and `n_members` columns. Since `%>%` takes
the object on its left and passes it as the first argument to the function on
its right, we don't need to explicitly include the data frame as an argument
to the `filter()` and `select()` functions any more.

Some may find it helpful to read the pipe like the word "then". For instance,
in the above example, we took the data frame `agreements`, *then* we `filter`ed
for rows with `n_members > 150`, *then* we `select`ed columns `agreement_name`, `year_signed`,
and `n_members`. The **`dplyr`** functions by themselves are somewhat simple,
but by combining them into linear workflows with the pipe, we can accomplish
more complex manipulations of data frames.

If we want to create a new object with this smaller version of the data, we
can assign it a new name. Let's also sort it with `arrange()`, putting the agreements with the most members first:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements_big <- agreements %>%
  filter(n_members > 150) %>%
  select(agreement_name, year_signed, n_members) %>%
  arrange(desc(n_members))

agreements_big
```

Note that the final data frame is the leftmost part of this expression. The most widely joined agreements are about desertification, the ozone layer, and climate change.

### Challenge
Using pipes, subset the `agreements` data to include agreements signed before
1950 and retain only the columns `year_signed`, `scope`, and `subject`. Name this dataframe `agreements_challenge`

<details>
<summary>ANSWER</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
agreements_challenge <- agreements %>%
    filter(year_signed < 1950) %>%
    select(year_signed, scope, subject)
```

## Mutate

Frequently you'll want to create new columns based on the values in existing
columns, for example to do unit conversions, or to find the difference between values in two
columns. For this we'll use `mutate()`.

To create a new column with the number of years it took each agreement to enter into force:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  mutate(years_to_force = year_in_force - year_signed)
```

You can also create a second new column based on the first new column within the same call of `mutate()`:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  mutate(years_to_force = year_in_force - year_signed,
         decades_to_force = years_to_force / 10)
```

If this runs off your screen and you just want to see the first few rows, you
can use a pipe to view the `head()` of the data. (Pipes work with non-**`dplyr`**
functions, too, as long as the **`dplyr`** or `magrittr` package is loaded).

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  mutate(years_to_force = year_in_force - year_signed) %>%
  select(agreement_name, year_signed, year_in_force, years_to_force) %>%
  head()
```

Some of these rows are `NA`, because those agreements never entered into force (or the IEA database doesn't know when they did). If we wanted to remove
those we could insert a `filter()` in the chain:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  filter(!is.na(year_in_force)) %>%
  mutate(years_to_force = year_in_force - year_signed) %>%
  select(agreement_name, year_signed, year_in_force, years_to_force) %>%
  head()
```

`is.na()` is a function that determines whether something is an `NA`. The `!`
symbol negates the result, so we're asking for every row where `year_in_force` *is not* an `NA`.

New columns are also a good way to check your data. An agreement can't take effect before it's signed, so `years_to_force` should never be negative. Is it?

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  mutate(years_to_force = year_in_force - year_signed) %>%
  filter(years_to_force < 0) %>%
  select(agreement_name, year_signed, year_in_force)
```

Two agreements say they entered into force before they were signed. One of them is off by almost a century, which looks like a typo in the original record. Real datasets have mistakes like this; a quick `mutate()` and `filter()` is often how you find them.

<div class = "blue">

### Challenge

Create a new data frame from the `agreements` data that meets the following
criteria: contains only the `agreement_name` column and a new column called
`years_to_force` containing the number of years between when the agreement was signed and when it entered into force.
In this `years_to_force` column, there are no `NA`s and all values are 10 or more (slow agreements!). Name this data frame `agreements_slow`.

**Hint**: think about how the commands should be ordered to produce this data frame!

<details>
<summary>ANSWER</summary>
```{r, eval=FALSE, purl=FALSE}
agreements_slow <- agreements %>%
    filter(!is.na(year_in_force)) %>%
    mutate(years_to_force = year_in_force - year_signed) %>%
    filter(years_to_force >= 10) %>%
    select(agreement_name, years_to_force)
```
</details>
</div>

## Group by and summarize

Many data analysis tasks can be approached using the *split-apply-combine*
paradigm: split the data into groups, apply some analysis to each group, and
then combine the results. **`dplyr`** makes this very easy through the use of the
`group_by()` function.

`group_by()` is often used together with `summarize()`, which collapses each
group into a single-row summary of that group.  `group_by()` takes as arguments
the column names that contain the **categorical** variables for which you want
to calculate the summary statistics. So to compute the mean number of members by scope:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  group_by(scope) %>%
  summarize(mean_members = mean(n_members, na.rm = TRUE))
```

No surprise that bilateral agreements average two members. What happens if you leave out `na.rm = TRUE`? Try it: a single `NA` in a group makes the whole mean `NA`.

You may also have noticed that the output from these calls doesn't run off the
screen anymore. It's one of the advantages of `tbl_df` over data frame.

You can also group by multiple columns:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  group_by(subject, scope) %>%
  summarize(mean_members = mean(n_members, na.rm = TRUE))
```

Multilateral agreements are much bigger than bilateral ones on every subject. But some rows say `NaN` ("not a number"). Every agreement in those groups is missing `n_members`, so once `na.rm = TRUE` removes the `NA`s there's nothing left to average.

We can also remove the missing values for `n_members` before we attempt to calculate the summary statistics. Because the missing values are removed first, we can omit `na.rm = TRUE` when computing the mean, and the all-`NA` groups drop out entirely:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  filter(!is.na(n_members)) %>%
  group_by(subject, scope) %>%
  summarize(mean_members = mean(n_members))
```

Here, again, the output from these calls doesn't run off the screen
anymore. If you want to display more data, you can use the `print()` function
at the end of your chain with the argument `n` specifying the number of rows to
display:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  filter(!is.na(n_members)) %>%
  group_by(subject, scope) %>%
  summarize(mean_members = mean(n_members)) %>%
  print(n = 15)
```

Once the data are grouped, you can also summarize multiple variables at the same
time (and not necessarily on the same variable). For instance, we could add a
column with the largest membership of any agreement in each group:

```{r, purl = FALSE}
agreements %>%
  filter(!is.na(n_members)) %>%
  group_by(subject, scope) %>%
  summarize(mean_members = mean(n_members),
            max_members = max(n_members))
```

<div class = "blue">

### Challenge

1. What was the largest number of members of any agreement signed in each year since 1990? Return a table with three columns: `year_signed`, the largest number of members (`max_members`), and that number as a percent of the 202 countries in the database (`max_pct`), arranged (`arrange()`) in descending order of `max_members`. (This table should have 36 rows, one for each year)
2. Try out a new function, `count()`. Group the data by `scope` and pipe the grouped data into the `count()` function. How could you get the same result using `group_by()` and `summarize()`? Hint: see `?n`.

<details>
<summary>ANSWER</summary>
```{r, purl=FALSE}
## Answer 1
agreements %>%
    filter(!is.na(n_members), year_signed >= 1990) %>%
    group_by(year_signed) %>%
    summarize(max_members = max(n_members)) %>%
    mutate(max_pct = max_members / 202 * 100) %>%
    arrange(desc(max_members))

## Answer 2
agreements %>%
  group_by(scope) %>%
  count()

agreements %>%
  group_by(scope) %>%
  summarize(n = n())
```
</details>
</div>
